pl-l4d3c1-d1e115.summary: Announces the next topics: what baptism is, its form, when it was instituted, and why.

pl-l4d3c1-d1e118.summary: Defines baptism as a dipping, an outward washing of the body done under the prescribed form of words. Without the word there is no sacrament; when the word comes to the element a sacrament is made, not the element itself but the washing done in the element.
claims: Baptism is an outward washing under the prescribed words.
Without the word there is no sacrament.
The washing, not the element, is the sacrament.

pl-l4d3c1-d1e121.summary: Quotes Augustine: baptism is consecrated by the word; take away the word, and what is water but water? The word comes to the element and it becomes a sacrament. The water's power to touch the body and wash the heart comes from the word, not because it is said but because it is believed; in the word the passing sound differs from the abiding power.
claims: The word consecrates the water of baptism.
The word works because it is believed, not merely spoken.

pl-l4d3c1-d1e131.summary: Concludes that baptism consists in word and element; though other things instituted for the sacrament's adornment are lacking, it is no less a true and holy sacrament if word and element are present. In this and other sacraments some things belong to adornment and dignity, others to substance and cause; word and element are of the substance, the rest pertain to its solemnity.
claims: Baptism consists in word and element.
Rites instituted for adornment are not necessary to the sacrament's validity.

pl-l4d3c1.summary: Sets out to treat what baptism is, its form, when it was instituted, and the reason for its institution. Baptism is a dipping, an outward washing of the body under the prescribed form of words; without the word there is no sacrament, but when the word is added to the element the washing, not the element itself, becomes the sacrament. Augustine: take away the word and water is only water; the word works not because it is said but because it is believed. Baptism therefore consists in word and element, which are its substance; other rites belong to its solemnity and their absence does not make it any less a true sacrament.
claims: Baptism is an outward washing under the prescribed form of words.
The washing, not the element, becomes the sacrament when the word is added.
Word and element are the substance of baptism; other rites belong to its solemnity.
